Vs. 
M/s G.M.G Corporation Ltd ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. Ruhul Islam J. I have gone through a copy of the judgment written by my learned brother Badrul Haider Chowdhury J. and the one written by my learned brother Shahabuddin Ahmed J. I concur with that of the latter. The question for consideration in this appeal is whether the mortgage deed submitted by the respondent for registration falls under Article 40(b) or Article (c) of the Stamp Act for the purpose of payment of stamp duty. The respondent G.M.G. Corporation Limited while enjoying cash credit facility with the Bank or Credit and Commerce International, briefly stated "BCCI" to the extent of Tk. 60,000,00/- (Taka sixty lacs) by executing a Demand Promissory Note and a deed of hypothecation of raw materials and finished goods as security, applied for raising the limit to Tk. 90,00,000/-. The bank allowed the respondent's prayer for raising the limit to Tk. 90,00,000/- and asked the respondent to execute a deed of mortgage in their favour in respect of their other movable and immovable properties by way of collateral/auxiliary security. The respondent executed a deed of mortgage to meet the requirement of the BCCI offering some immovable properties as the additional security after obtaining no objection clearance from the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, with which the properties were mortgaged. The mortgage deed was presented for registration with stamp duty calculated under clause (p) of Article 40. A question was raised that the mortgage deed was not executed by way of collateral or auxiliary security but it was a primary or principal security, and stamp duty is leviable under clause (b) of Article 40. A Special Bench of the High Court Division heard the reference made by the National Board of Revenue under section 51 of the- Stamp Act and rejected the contention of the taxing authorities and held that the mortgage deed in question was a collateral/auxiliary security chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40 of the Stamp Act; and the National Board of Revenue by special leave preferred this appeal. The correspondence between the bank and the respondent and the recitals in the mortgage deed clearly support the plea of the respondent that under the mortgage deed some movable and immovable properties are being offered by way of collateral/auxiliary security against the cash credit facility of Tk. 90,00,000/-. It is not the case that the security is being offered against the specified amount of loan of Tk. 90,00,000/- but it is by way of security against the cash credit facility having the limit at Tk. 90,00,000/-, The Demand Promissory Note and the Deed of Hypothecation together construe a mortgage as contemplated under the Stamp Act. The bank, as per terms of the mortgage deed, can fall upon the mortgaged property only when the primary security, namely, the Demand Promissory Note and the Deed of Hypothecation fall short to satisfy the outstanding demand of the bank. In the face of clear recital in the deed in question I find it difficult to accept the contention of the appellant that the mortgage in this case falls under the category of primary or principal security. The deed as drawn up clearly falls in the category of collateral/auxiliary, in' as much as some immovable properties are being offered as collateral/auxiliary or additional security for the cash credit facility raised to the extent of Tk.90.00.000/- in favour of the respondent, and stamp duty is chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40. In my view the Special Bench of the High Court Division has correctly answered the question, mid the appeal must fail. Therefore the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

 Badrul Haider Chowdhuiy J. —This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the Special Bench of the High Court Division passed in Reference Case No. 1 of 1981 under section 57 of the Stamp Act, 1899.

 13. The distinction between Article 6 and Article 40 is that Article 6 islimited to causes where a loan is in question and Article 40 cover the cases where interest in or rights over property is transferred whether possession is delivered or not as security for the mortgage money. For the purpose of as curtaining which of the articles is attracted the document in question is to be seen. When although words 'pledge' was used in the instrument the document taken as a while the transaction really appeared to be a transfer by way of mortgage, it was held in 21 Cal 241 that the document was a deed of mortgage chargeable under Article 40. 

 Where the Mortgagor gives to the mortgagee a Power of Attorney to collect rent of a lease of the property mortgaged or part thereof is deemed to give possession within the meaning of this Article. That means in such case it will come under clause (a) and not (b). 

 16. Rate of duty is less in such circumstances. The instrument in question though drafted in the language which says: "This is a collateral or auxiliary security" and mentioned about "second mortgage". This does not really come under clause (c) because it is not the case here the "principal or primary security is duly tamped". 

 There is no principal or primary security in the present case which was duly stamped. The only document that was executed was the document of hypothecation and pledge. The expression 'for the above mentioned purpose' can only mean mortgage. The respondent has given mortgage for the first time to the Bank of Credit and Commerce though the respondent has taken previously a cash credit facility by executing promissory note by hypothecation of their goods or pledges which are governed by Article 6. The present instrument cannot be a collateral security because the present instrument is a mortgage deed and it does not relate to any previous mortgage which has been given to the Bank of Credit and Commerce Ltd. Had it been the case that the present mortgage was intended to be a second mortgage to the Shilpa Rin Sangstha, then it could be argued that the present document is merely a collateral security or auxiliary or additional or substituted security by way of further assurance because the principal and primary security is already stamped, namely, first mortgage deed but that is not the case. It is perfectly clear that the object of the instrument was to give to the Bank some rights by way of security. This is not a deed of hypothecation. Therefore it comes under Article 40(b). Reliance may be placed on the case of Secretary to the Commission of Salt etc. Madras V. Mrs. Orr 38 Mad 646 for this proposition. Next, in the case of failure to adjust the loan the respondent covenanted that "the bank shall be entitled to take possession of the schedule properties and/or appoint a Manager or Receiver without intervention of the Court" and further the Bank shall be at liberty to sell the scheduled property". 

 17. It is well settled that the question of what stamp duty is payable on a document must necessarily be decided on the words of the document and the terms it embodies. Reliance may be placed on a Board of Revenue Vs. Sorrarazu AIR 1976 Mad 1038 (FB) where the Court considered whether a document fell under clause (a) or (b) explaining the words "agreed to be given". It was held that the document in' that case came under clause (b) of section 33 of the Madras Stamp Act. This is the first mortgage so far as the Bank of Credit and Commerce is concerned and in this deed possession has not been given. Therefore, the document comes within clause (b) and not (c). 

 18. Article (c) deals with a case in which a separate instrument offered an additional or substituted security is executed subsequent to the original mortgage transaction which had been reduced into writing in a previously completed instrument. The respondents have executed promissory note for the purpose of hypothecation to the Bank of Credit and Commerce but the present document is the first document which is being given as a mortgage deed and therefore it could not be said that the present document is executed subsequent to the original mortgage transaction. No such mortgage transaction had taken place previously between the Bank and the respondent. In the case of Mutual Property Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Inland Revenue Commissioner, 196 All England Reports 493 the question was when the second mortgage of freehold property was subject to an existing 6rst mortgage by the mortgagor to a third party contained a covenant by the borrower to pay the second mortgagees by installments under certain circumstances and whether the first mortgage had been duly stamped with the appropriate duty on the amount thereby secured, the set mortgage deed was primary security. It was held as between the mortgagor and the second mortgagees that the instrument was the primary security for the obligation which those parties had created between themselves and was not secondary to the mortgagor's obligation towards the first mortgage, nor was the covenant by the mortgagor to pay to the second mortgagees the amount of the first mortgage merely auxiliary to the first mortgage, It was observed that the appellants were not paying duty twice on the same sum because the sums concerned in the first and second mortgages constituted different obligations between different parties, and the instrument was liable to stamp duty either as a mortgage or as a covenant within Schd. I to the Stamp Act, 1891, on the aggregate of the sums secured by the two mortgagees. 

 19. This case is on all fours with the present case. Here the mortgagor (sic) was the Shilpa Rin Sangstha and the second mortgage was with BCCI Ltd. The two are entirely different obligations between different parties and therefore clause (c) by no stretch of imagination can come into play to show that the mortgage deed which has been offered by the respondent to the BCCI is auxiliary or additional or by way of further assurance to another primary security. There was no primary security; there was only a hypothecation by the Company to the Bank for cash credit limit and the rate of duty is less under Article 6 whereas when the company wanted to raise the cash credit limit to 90 lacs the Bank asked for security by way of mortgage of moveables and immovable. This was clearly done by the present instrument and therefore it has to be stamped as a mortgage deed because that is all it is. It was done so expressly. There is no scope for interpretation of written document which the parties have expressly put into in writing: There is no question of construing the document favourable to the subject. It is the document between two individual parties and they bargained for what they wanted to do. The only question is what is the rate of duty that should be paid To bring such document within the fold of document purported to be a document of hypothecation is to adopt a process of reasoning which is not sanctioned by law nor the document itself allows such scope. It says that it is deed of mortgage, if it is, as it is, it is not conceivable how the document can escape from being stamped under other than clause (b). 

 20A. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed argued that the present document is a collateral or additional document by way of further assurance for enhancing the cash credit limit but when questioned about the principal or primary security which is duly stamped he had no answer. The execution of hypothecation and the Promissory notes are chargeable under a different article namely article 6 which provides for lesser rate of stamp duty but in the case of mortgage the duty is higher. 

 21. Abdul Wadud Bhuiya, the learned Additional Attorney General placed before us the entire document and the relevant portions of which have already been quoted earlier in this judgment. Reliance was placed on the decision of Inland Revenue Commissioner V. Hanny Ansbacher & co. (1962) 3 All ER 843 where the House of Lords considered a similar point as to the Stamp duty. In that case the respondents by agreement agreed to purchase all the Ordinary stock of a company for a price payable in two installments. The first installment was duly paid. The second remained outstanding. By Cl. II of the sale agreement the respondent agreed to procure that the sum payable as the second installment should be guaranteed to the extent of 750,000 by a bank. The stamp duty payable on this guarantee was passed at dollars' 1,875 (5 shilling for every dollars 100 of dollar 750,000) on the ground that the guarantee came within the heading "mortgage, bond, debenture, covenant being the only or principal or primary security for the payment or repayment of money in Sch. I to the Stamp Act, 1899" It was held that the guarantee was collateral security to a primary security (the Sale agreement), the primary obligation for payment was that of the respondent under the sale agreement and that was exempt from stamp duty. Therefore, the collateral security, viz. the guarantee, attracted maximum duty of 10 Shillings. 

 22. This decision reinforces the view taken by us that the mortgage-deed in question could not be taken as a collateral security inasmuch as there is no primary or principal security in this case. The position emerges that the document in question is a mortgage deed and that is the first mortgage which has been offered to the Bank of Credit and Commerce and therefore it is changeable under clause (b). It does not come by any stretch of imagination under clause (c) 

 24. Facts of the case having been already set out and discussed in the judgment of my learned brother I shall only touch on them briefly to explain my view. The respondent, a Manufacturing Industry, obtained, and was already enjoying a loan, up to the limit of Tk.60 (sixty) lacs which was later on raised to Tk. 90 (ninety) lacs, from the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, briefly BCCI, by executing a demand promissory note and a deed of hypothecation of raw materials and finished goods in favour of the BCCI as security for the payment of the loan. The BCCI thereafter asked, the respondent to execute a deed of mortgage in their favour in respect of other movable and immovable properties of the respondent by way of collateral auxiliary 'security for repayment of the' loan. Accordingly, the respondent executed the deed of mortgage in question after having taken permission of another mortgagee, the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangsiha, to whom the same properties had already been mortgaged as a security for some other advance of money The respondent paid stamp duty of Tk. 27,000/- (Twenty seven thousand on this mortgage-deed, computed under clause (c) of Article 40 and presented it for registration before the Sub-registrar But the Sub registrar" contended that the mortgage deed was not a collateral or auxiliary security but it  was a primary or principal security, and as such, it was chargeable at the higher rate as prescribed under clause (b) of Article 40. In this way the controversy arose which was ultimately referred to the Special Bench of the High Court Division constituted with three Judges under section 57 of the Stamp Act. The Special Bench after hearing the parties rejected the 'contention of the taxing authorities, namely the National Board of Revenue and held that the mortgage deed was a collateral/auxiliary security chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40. Against this decision of the Special 'Bench of the High Court Division the National Board of Revenue preferred this appeal by special leave granted by us. 

 25. Schedule I of the Stamp Act is a list of various instruments which are chargeable with duties it different rates as prescribed in the said Schedule. A Mortgage-Deed has been listed against Article 40 of this Schedule. The mortgage deed in question in this case, executed by the respondent in favour of the Beer, being an instrument for securing loan is chargeable under Article 40. Mortgage deeds are chargeable at three different rates as prescribed under clauses (a), (b) and (c) of this Article according to their nature or classification. When possession' of the property which is subject' matter of the mortgage deed is given or agreed to be given by the mortgagor, the mortgage deed will be charge at the rate prescribed under clause (a); this rate is "the same duty as a Conveyance for a consideration equal to the amount secured by such deed," Admittedly, under the mortgage deed in question no possession of the property is given and, as such, clause (a) will not apply thereto. Clause (b) will apply to a mortgage deed when possession is not given or agreed to be given; the rate under this clause is "the same duty as a bond under Article 15 for the amount secured by such deed. At the moment, this rate is two percent of the amount of loan secured by the mortgage deed and computed there under the duty of this mortgage-deed will be Taka one lac eighty thousand. Clause (c) will apply to a mortgage deed if constitutes "a collateral or auxiliary or additional or substituted security or by way of further assurance" for repayment of a loan; rate under this clause is much less- i.e. fifty paisa" for every sum secured not exceeding Tk. 1,000.00; computed on this basis the duty of this mortgage deed comes to taka twenty seven thousand which the respondent has already paid as mentioned above. 

 26. Appellant's contention is that the 'mortgage deed is- not a collateral/auxiliary additional security but it is a primary or principal security against the loan advanced to respondent in that the demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation which are claimed by the respondent to be tile primary or principal security are not a mortgage-deed duly stamped under clause (a) or clause (b) of Article 40. The mortgage deed in question is therefore the primary security chargeable under clause (b). Respondent's contention is that when the loan has already been taken against the security by way of the demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation of goods which have also been duly stamped, the demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation, are 'necessarily the primary security, and the mortgage deed being required as security in addition to the promissory note and the deed of hypothecation the mortgage deed is nothing but collateral/auxiliary security. A collateral or auxiliary security is a security which is furnished in addition to a security already furnished; a collateral or auxiliary security is enforceable only when the primary security after being enforced falls short of meeting the obligation to repay the loan. There is no dispute that unless there is a primary principal security the question of collateral or auxiliary security cannot arise. In this case the loan was already obtained against the security of a demand promissory note and a deed of hypothecation of goods and these two securities were also duly stamped under Article 6 of Schedule I. Secondly, the Mortgage- deed describes itself as a 'collateral/auxiliary security"; it records that the mortgagee, namely the BCCI required "mortgage" of other assets and landed properties of the borrower as "collateral/auxiliary security" in addition to the security already furnished by execution of the promissory note and the deed of hypothecation. Paragraph IV e) of the mortgage deed reads thus: 

 27. The learned Additional Attorney- General appearing for the appellant opened his arguments with a misconception of the respondent's case. He thought that the respondents treated their previous mortgage in favour of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangsthea’s the 'primary security and their later mortgage in favour of the BCCI as the "secondary security" and" accordingly argued that these two mortgages to different persons for different sums of money are independent of each other and that the later one cannot be secondary to the earlier one, both being the "primary security". In support of this argument the learned Additional Attorney General has referred to the case Mutual Property Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Inland Revenue Commissioner 1926 All Eng. Rep. 493. There is no question that mortgages to two different persons or organization’s -for meeting different obligations are independent of each other, and that they constitute "primary security". But this is not at all the case of the respondent here. The respondents never claim that their mortgage to the BCCI is secondary in relation to their earlier mortgage to the BSRS. Their case is that their mortgage to the BCCI is secondary security in relation to their demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation executed in favour of the BCCI. As such this decision as referred to has got no relevance to the instant case. The fact that the respondent had previously mortgaged the same properties to the BSRS or, for that purpose, to any other person, is irrelevant in the instant case For, so long the value of the property mortgaged is sufficiently high to cover the obligation under both the mortgages, and if the prior mortgagee has no objection to the subsequent mortgage, the mortgagor is at liberty to mortgage the same property to different persons. The question involved in this case is whether the Mortgage Deed in question is a collateral security in relation to the security by way of the demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation, both the securities being in favour of the same 'lender and in respect of the same loan". It must be borne in mind that the primary security and the collateral security as mentioned in clause (c) are necessarily against the same loan. 

 30. Faqeer Shahabuddin Ahmed learned Advocate for the respondent has strongly defended the High Court Division's decision citing a number of decisions' including one from the English jurisdiction. In "National Bank of Pakistan Vs. Fasihuzzaman" PLD 1964 KAR-92, a Special Bench of the West Pakistan High Court constituted under section 57 of the Stamp Act" considered a similar question A loan of Rs. six thousand was advanced by the National Bank to the respondent against a promissory note which was stamped under the Stamp Act; thereafter the Bank required of the respondent to execute a mortgage deed covering his landed property in addition to the promissory note as a secondary note security. Same objection was taken in that case as has been taken before us that the promissory note did not constitute primary security but the mortgage deed was in fact the principal or primary security chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40. Alternatively it was contended, if the promissory note were the primary security it must be stamped as a mortgage deed under clause (a) or clause (b). The Special Bench overruled this contention and held that the promissory note was the primary or principal security and the mortgage dead was its collateral or principal security chargeable under clause (c) with an observation that the language of clause (c) cannot be so stretched as to indicate that 'primary security' should be also a mortgage deed. The other cases cited by Faqeer Shahabuddin Ahmed need not be discussed here as reference to those cases was made in this Karachi Bench case. 

 31. In ''Inland Revenue Commissioners Vs. Henry Ansbacher &Co.", All-Eng. Rep. 1962 (3) P. 843, the House of Lords considered a similar question in an appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal. That was a case under Schedule I of the Stamp Act, 1891 of which our Stamp Act, 1899 may be called an exact replica. The respondent in that case purchased the originally stock of a Company at a price to be paid in two installments. The first installment was paid at once and for the second installment he executed an agreement- "sale agreement." The creditor required a Bank guarantee also which was then furnished. The stamp duty payable on this guarantee was assessed at £ 1,875 on the ground that the guarantee came within the heading "Mortgage, bond debenture, covenant" being the only or principal or primary security for the payment or repayment of money. This contention of the taxing authorities was rejected by the Court which held the bank guarantee to be a collateral security, that is, a security in addition to the sale agreement which was held to be the primary security. House of Lords observed: 

 32. On consideration of the arguments advanced and on interpretation of clause (c) I hold that the Mortgage-deed in question is a collateral/auxiliary security ill relation to the Demand Promissory Note and the Hypothecation deed which' are the primary and principal security for repayment of the same loan and as such this Mortgage-deed is chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40. The Special Bench of the High Court Division is found to have correctly decided the question of law on proper appreciation of facts of the case.
